title: Friendly to all
hook: Krishna: dear to me is one who hates no being, friendly and compassionate (Bhagavad Gita 12.13)
carry: a stranger at a bus stop

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gita Govinda, and the flute calling through the trees. Your line was the flute. What beautiful thing did you let call to you? Today, Krishna speaks again, and this time about whom he holds dear. Day eight hundred forty-four.

A battlefield, two armies facing each other, and in the space between them a chariot. The warrior Arjuna has lost his nerve, and his charioteer, Krishna, is talking him through it. That conversation is the Bhagavad Gita. By its twelfth chapter, Arjuna has seen a vision of Krishna's cosmic form, and now he asks a quieter question: who knows yoga better, those who worship Krishna in a form, or those who worship the formless? Krishna's answer winds toward something that isn't a ritual or a rank. It's a portrait of a person. And the portrait starts with one who hates no being. Today: friendly to all.
screen: `A CHARIOT BETWEEN ARMIES.` → `ARJUNA ASKS A QUIET QUESTION.` → `A PORTRAIT OF A PERSON.`

segments.voice: First, the verse. Krishna says, in paraphrase: the one who hates no being, who is friendly and compassionate, free from the sense of mine and free from ego, the same in pain and pleasure, and forgiving, that devotee is dear to me. Notice where it starts. Not with prayer, not with sacrifice. With hating no one. Second, the word friendly. In Sanskrit it's maitra. The verse doesn't say friends with all, as if everyone becomes your best friend. It says friendly: a basic warmth toward every being, the default setting of the heart. And right beside it stands compassion, karuna, which feels for those who suffer. Third, free from mine. The same verse joins friendliness to letting go of possessiveness and ego. Some readers hear a link there: unfriendliness can grow out of mine. My seat, my way, my turn. When the grip on mine loosens, there's more room to be friendly. Fourth, dear to God. Earlier in the Gita, Krishna speaks of devotion as offering. Here he says who is dear to him: the person whose love has spilled outward into how they treat every creature. Devotion to God, in this verse, shows up as friendliness to everyone else. A stranger at a bus stop becomes, in this light, part of the practice.
screen: `THE VERSE: HATING NO BEING.` · `MAITRA: FRIENDLY.` · `FREE FROM MINE.` · `DEAR TO GOD.` · then, large: `FRIENDLY TO ALL.`

segments.voice: Sit and let your breath settle. Bring to mind a stranger you saw recently. Someone in line, a driver, a person walking a dog. You don't know their name or their story. Picture their face as well as you can. Now, gently, let yourself be friendly toward them. Not loving, not attached, just warm. The way you'd nod at a neighbor. Hold that warmth for a few breaths. Then picture passing them again tomorrow, and the nod you'd give. If you pray, you can hold them in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Maitra. The Sanskrit word for a basic warmth toward every being, the devotee's friendliness that Krishna calls dear to him. Today's word.
Your line: a stranger at a bus stop. Once today, be friendly to a stranger: a nod, a held door, a real thank you. Day eight hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Hindus read and recite the Bhagavad Gita at home, in temples and in study groups, and its twelfth chapter, on devotion, is sometimes recited on its own.

fork.setup: Krishna paints a portrait of the devotee dear to him. what comes first in it?
options: one who performs the most sacrifices.
one who hates no being, friendly and compassionate.
one who knows the most scripture.
fork.reveal: his portrait begins with hating no being: friendliness and compassion, freedom from mine.

original.note: Sanskrit: friendly, the word in Gita 12.13, set beside karuṇa, compassionate.

trapdoor: what you thought: be nice to everyone.
what it means: a warmth toward every being, tied to letting go of mine, that makes a devotee dear to God.
what a scholar hears: adveṣṭā sarva-bhūtānāṁ maitraḥ karuṇa eva ca, the opening of Krishna's portrait in Gita 12.13.

notes: Gita 12.13 is paraphrased; some translators place 'same in pain and pleasure, forgiving' in 12.13 and others carry it into 12.14. Confirm the verse division.
Arnold 1885 is on the validator list but its exact wording for 12.13 was not certain, so it is not quoted.
'Earlier in the Gita, Krishna speaks of devotion as offering' refers to 9.26; confirm.
Sanskrit transliteration in the trapdoor and the form maitraḥ should be checked.
'Its twelfth chapter is often recited on its own' in howItsDone is a general claim; confirm or soften.

Editor: Arjuna's 12.1 question is about which worshippers are best and the portrait comes later, so hook and fork are reworded; cut the narrator's 'a great deal of unfriendliness' claim; the practice no longer widens the circle (846 does that); source ref widened to 12.13–14, where 'dear to me' falls.
Audit: Arjuna's question in 12.1 now follows the text (worship of Krishna in form or of the unmanifest, and who knows yoga better); the narrator's 'the verse suggests' is now 'some readers hear'.
